pages.c17-p03: Test a model using separate test data, accuracy and a confusion matrix

pages.c17-p06: Plan a machine learning solution to a real problem, including data, testing and ethics

q.q: What is machine learning?
o: Computers learning patterns from data instead of following hand-written rules

q.q: What is supervised learning?
o: Learning from examples labelled with the correct answers
Learning by trial and error in a game

q.q: In a dataset about animals, "number of legs" is a...
In a dataset about animals, "bird" is a...
q.why: The label is the category to predict.

q.q: What is a dataset?
Why is ML useful for recognising cats in photos?
o: It's very hard to write exact rules for recognising cats
Cats are always the same colour
q.why: Learning from examples replaces impossible rules.

q.q: What happens during training?
o: The model adjusts itself to reduce mistakes on the examples

q.q: A model says "dog: 87%". What is the 87%?
o: How many dogs it has seen

q.q: For images, what are the features?
Which is a traditional program rather than ML?
o: A program with rules written by a programmer
A spam filter learned from examples
A speech recogniser trained on recordings

q.q: What does a classifier do?
What is a class in a classifier?
o: One of the categories it can choose

q.q: Which is an example of a classifier?
What is the golden rule of machine learning?
o: A model can only be as good as its data

q.q: About how many examples per class should you start with in Teachable Machine?
q.why: More examples help the model learn.

q.q: Why should training images be varied?
o: So the model learns the object, not one setting

q.q: What does "balanced classes" mean?
o: A similar number of examples in each class

q.q: Why add a "nothing" class?
o: So the model can say nothing is there instead of guessing
Because there must be three classes

q.q: Your model fails when objects are far away. What should you do?
o: Add training examples taken from further away
Only use objects close up forever

q.q: Why shouldn't you train school models on pupils' faces?
o: Face data is personal and sensitive

q.q: What is test data?
o: Examples kept separate to check the model on new data

q.q: Why test on data the model hasn't seen?
o: To find out how it will do on new examples

q.q: A typical split for training and test data is...
q.why: Most data trains; some is held back.

q.q: What is accuracy?
o: The percentage of predictions that are correct

q.q: A model gets 45 out of 50 right. Its accuracy is...
A model gets 30 out of 40 right. Its accuracy is...
What does a confusion matrix show?
o: Which classes the model gets right and which it mixes up
q.why: It compares actual and predicted classes.

q.q: In a confusion matrix, correct predictions appear...
q.why: Actual matches predicted on the diagonal.

q.q: Why can accuracy be misleading for rare events?
o: A model can score high by always predicting the common class
q.why: E.g. always "not spam" can look accurate.

q.q: Testing a model on its training data is like...
o: sitting an exam you've already seen the answers to

q.q: A confusion matrix shows many "paper" items predicted as "plastic". What should you do?
o: Add more varied examples of paper and plastic

q.q: What is overfitting?
o: Memorising training data so the model fails on new data
A model that is too fast

q.q: Which result suggests overfitting?
What does it mean for a model to generalise?
o: It works only on training data
It works well on new examples

q.q: What is shortcut learning?
o: Using an accidental clue instead of the real feature

q.q: A wolf detector actually learned to detect snow. Why?
o: Most wolf photos had snow in the background
q.why: The background was an accidental clue.

q.q: What is an edge case?
o: An unusual situation rarely in the training data

q.q: Why do self-driving cars need huge amounts of testing?
o: Real roads are full of unusual edge cases

q.q: What is underfitting?
o: The model hasn't learned the patterns well enough

q.q: Which helps make a model more robust?
o: Collecting more varied data and testing on realistic data

q.q: Why keep humans involved in safety-critical AI?
o: Mistakes can be dangerous, so people need to check

q.q: All "good" fruit photos were taken in daylight and "bad" ones at night. What might the model learn?
o: The real signs of bad fruit
q.why: It may learn a lighting shortcut.

q.q: What is bias in machine learning?
o: When a model is less accurate or fair for some people

q.q: Where does AI bias usually come from?
What is under-representation?
o: When some groups barely appear in the data

q.q: What is historical bias?
o: Data that reflects unfair decisions from the past
Ancient datasets that are always accurate

q.q: What is labelling bias?
o: When the people labelling data add their own assumptions
Using labels that are too long

q.q: Research found some face-analysis systems were least accurate for...
q.why: The Gender Shades study showed this gap.

q.q: Why did an experimental CV-sorting AI prefer male applicants?
o: It learned from past hires who were mostly men

q.q: What is representative data?
o: Data with a fair mix of everyone the system will meet

q.q: Why test accuracy separately for different groups?
o: Overall accuracy can hide poor accuracy for some groups

q.q: Which helps reduce bias?
o: Including people from different backgrounds in the team

q.q: A soap dispenser sensor doesn't detect darker skin. The likely cause is...
o: It wasn't tested on a range of skin tones
The sensor is broken for everyone
q.why: Narrow testing leads to unfair products.

q.q: Which statement about unfair AI is most accurate?
o: It usually comes from data, not someone programming it to be unfair

q.q: What is the first stage of an ML project?
q.why: Start with a clear problem statement.

q.q: What is a problem statement?
o: A clear description of the problem and who it's for

q.q: When is ML NOT the best solution?
o: When a simple rule solves the problem
q.why: Simple rules are cheaper and clearer.

q.q: What is evaluation?
o: Judging how well a solution works against success criteria

q.q: Why decide success criteria before testing?
o: To judge results fairly and honestly
q.why: Deciding first avoids moving the goalposts.

q.q: What is human oversight?
o: People checking and able to overrule AI decisions

q.q: Why keep monitoring a model after launch?
o: Real-world data can change and accuracy can drop

q.q: Which is an important privacy question for an ML project?
o: Did people agree to their data being used?

q.q: Which is a fairness question for an ML project?
o: Does it work equally well for everyone?
Does it use the newest chip?

q.q: In a medical AI, which mistake is often worse?
o: A false alarm that's quickly checked

q.q: What does "deploy" mean in an ML project?
o: Put the model into real use

q.q: Which is the best reason to involve users in testing?
o: They show how it works in real conditions

q.q: Which is NOT a good source of training data?
o: Photos of people taken without permission

q.q: Which describes the ML project cycle?
o: Define, collect data, train, test, evaluate, deploy and monitor

q.q: A model is 95% accurate overall but 70% for one group. What should you do?
o: Investigate and improve the data for that group before using it

q.q: What is the main job of the label column in training data?
o: Give the correct answer for each example

q.q: Which is an example of supervised learning?
o: Training a model on emails marked "spam" or "not spam"

q.q: What does Teachable Machine let you do?
o: Train a simple ML model in your browser

q.q: You trained with only your own hand. Why might it fail for a friend?
o: Their hand looks different and wasn't in the data
q.why: Lack of variety limits the model.

q.q: What is a false positive?
o: The model says "yes" when the real answer is "no"
q.why: E.g. flagging a real email as spam.

q.q: What is a false negative?
o: The model says "no" when the real answer is "yes"
q.why: E.g. missing a real spam email.

q.q: In a confusion matrix of 30 items, 24 are on the diagonal. The accuracy is...
Which is a sign of good generalisation?
o: Perfect training accuracy, poor test accuracy
Similar accuracy on training and test data

q.q: What should you do to avoid shortcut learning?
o: Vary backgrounds and conditions across all classes

q.q: Who might be harmed if a school face-recognition door had biased data?
Which action helps make data more representative?
o: Collecting examples from groups that are missing

q.q: Which is a responsible way to collect data for a school ML project?
o: Ask permission and avoid collecting personal data you don't need

q.q: What does it mean if a model "drifts"?
o: Its accuracy falls as the real world changes

q.q: What does ML stand for?
Which is the BEST description of training data for a classifier?
o: Varied, balanced, correctly labelled examples of each class

q.q: A model labels every test item as the most common class. What is likely wrong?
o: The classes were unbalanced in training

q.q: Why is a 99% accurate cancer screening AI not automatically safe to use?
o: 99% is too low for any use
It could still miss rare cancers, so mistakes must be checked

q.q: Which describes human-in-the-loop AI?
o: A robot with a human body
A person reviews the AI's important decisions
q.why: Humans stay in the decision process.

q.q: Which job title belongs to someone who builds and trains ML models?
A model to sort fruit sees an orange-coloured apple. This is an example of...
In the fruit dataset, how many features does an example with weight, colour and skin texture have?
q.why: Three pieces of information are features; the label is separate.

q.q: Which of these is a label for a weather model?
q.why: Labels are what we predict; the rest are features.

q.q: What does pressing "Train" in Teachable Machine do?
o: It uploads images to social media
The model learns patterns from your example images

q.q: Which classes would suit a hand-gesture classifier for a slide clicker?
A recycling sorter scored 9/10 for paper, 6/10 for plastic and 10/10 for nothing. Which class needs work?
Why might you keep the test data hidden even from yourself while improving the model?
o: So you don't accidentally tune the model to the test
q.why: Peeking makes test scores too optimistic.

q.q: A model memorises that every training cat photo has a red blanket. On a new cat with no blanket it fails. This is...
q.why: It learned the blanket, not the cat.

q.q: Which is the best way to find edge cases?
A dataset of voices has mostly adults. What might the model struggle with?
Which is an example of fairness testing?
o: Checking accuracy for pupils of every year group separately
q.why: Test each group, not just the average.

q.q: For a lost-property classifier, which is the best success criterion?
o: At least 85% test accuracy for every class
